description: Hi! I’m Taimour, a CS undergrad (FUUAST, Islamabad) focused on trustworthy AI for health data. I’ve done 4 AI/ML internships and build models that explain their decisions and flag when they’re unsure. We’ll build an astronaut health monitor that spots anomalies in vitals (heart rate, SpO2, sleep) and explains every alert. Looking for: a frontend/dashboard dev (React or Streamlit), someone into biomedical or space-health data, and a designer for our demo video. Let’s build!
summary: Aurafex is health-monitoring software that lets astronauts on long missions check their own health and act on it without waiting for Earth. A two-minute daily self-check, plus wearable and vehicle sensors, collects vitals, sleep, exercise, mood, symptoms, cabin CO₂ and radiation dose. Aurafex compares each astronaut with their own pre-flight baseline and with NASA limits (NASA-STD-3001). It then rates seven health areas GO, WATCH or ACT. Every alert explains why it fired, states how confident it is, and gives clear steps to take now. Distance from Earth means astronauts must be their own first line of detection, and Aurafex gives them a tool they can understand and trust, even offline
details:
What it does Aurafex is an on-board health self-monitoring app for long-duration missions such as Mars transit. It covers seven health areas linked to NASA's spaceflight hazards: heart & circulation, bone & muscle, mind & mood, sleep & fatigue, immune system, radiation, and cabin air (CO₂).

  1. Gather: A two-minute daily self-check records resting heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature, body mass, aerobic and resistive exercise, sleep, 1–5 ratings for sleep quality, mood, stress and fatigue, and symptoms (headache, blurred vision, congestion, cold sore, rash, back pain, nausea). Vehicle sensors add cabin CO₂ and radiation dose.
  2. Compare to "your normal": Each astronaut has a baseline built from pre-flight days. Aurafex compares 7-day averages against that personal baseline, because an individual change can be hidden inside population averages.
  3. Check NASA limits: Rules from NASA standards can raise an alert. Cabin CO₂ above 3 mmHg means ACT; a 7-day average above 2.5 mmHg means WATCH. A radiation spike (solar particle event) or a projected career dose near the 600 mSv limit also raises an alert, as do body-mass loss and low resistive-exercise adherence for bone and muscle.
  4. Explain, with honesty about uncertainty: Every alert lists the readings behind it (e.g. "Resting heart rate 7-day average 66 bpm vs your pre-flight 58 bpm, 5.3 SD higher"). Every area shows a confidence score based on how much data was actually logged. When data is missing, Aurafex says so instead of showing a false "all clear". The bone-density estimate is shown as a range based on NASA's 1–1.5%/month evidence, not as a single number.
  5. Act: Each WATCH or ACT comes with concrete steps (e.g. "move to the storm shelter, postpone EVA") and clear "don't wait for the app" emergency criteria. A one-click report for the flight surgeon is queued for the next communication window.

How it works Aurafex is a single, dependency-free HTML/JavaScript web app that runs entirely in the browser, so it works offline. It must keep working when Earth is up to 22 light-minutes away. The demo runs a synthetic 180-day Mars-transit mission for two fictional crew members, with six scenarios: CO₂ removal degraded, isolation stress, missing data, a solar particle event, immune symptoms, and an exercise-device fault. The app has five simple tabs: Today (a health ring and the top priority), Health areas (why and what to do), Daily check-in, Mission (a colour map of the whole mission that judges can play through), and How it works. Saving a check-in updates the assessment instantly.

Benefits

  • Earlier detection: personal baselines catch changes that population thresholds would miss.
  • Trust: explanations and confidence scores let astronauts decide whether to act.
  • Autonomy: on-board, offline guidance for when ground support is delayed.
  • Less noise: we tuned the logic so that calm mission days stay GO; a missed workout alone never triggers an alert.

What we hope to achieve We want to show that crew health tools should be explainable and honest about what they don't know. Next steps: connect real wearables and vehicle telemetry, validate thresholds on real flight data (e.g. NASA's Open Science Data Repository), and add a privacy-preserving whole-crew view. The same approach could help people on Earth who live far from medical care.

Tools used HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks), GitHub Pages for hosting, Python + Playwright for automated testing of alert behaviour across all 180 mission days, and Claude Slides for the demo deck.
